doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Drummers, bandmates and the rhythm section
summary: He lists the drummers and the long-serving horn players, and explains the bass and drums carried the time with no rhythm guitar.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Who was the drummer when you joined?

We had several. Sam Woodyard was the first one that I worked with. Then Louie came in. Then there was Rufus Jones, and then there was the other Jones, Elvin Jones was there for a short time. Yeah I was amazed too. And there was another fella that he used, Chris Columbo — not Columbo, it’s Columbus. Chris Columbus or Columbo. A fellow out of Atlantic City. Chris, I call him Chris. But he was president of the local there for a while, and he worked with the band for a while. And there were several others that sat in briefly. And it just went on and on. And sometimes we’d have substitutes too. You ever hear of a guy by the name of Dollar Brand?
He had his first gig with Duke.
He’s from South Africa isn’t he?

Yeah. And there was a guy by the name of Wolf Freeman who was from South Africa, a bass player. He used to come in, he had to come in by way of Canada and then to the United States. And I used to see him out there at Basin Street all the time.
There seemed to be quite a turnover, at least in the drum chair.
Well not really. They were just substitutes. Short term players. It’s in this book here. He kept the same people, he had the same saxophone section the whole time I was there.
I’m sure you are familiar with all of those players.

And the same trombone players including Buster Cooper, he lives in town here, he lives in St. Pete. And Chuck Conners and Lawrence Brown. And Cootie and Cat Anderson and sometimes he had Ray Nance and he had Money Johnson sometimes and he had Mercer, who was the business manager as well. There was Herbie Jones. And the weight of the band most of the time was on the drummer and myself as far as keeping time. So I just kept that time.
Right. There was no rhythm guitar.
And Duke didn’t always play all that much.

No not all the time, no. And whatever he put up there, I had to be observant enough to catch it, either from his keyboard, from listening to the band, or from reading something that they had written out, they had sketched out something. I had to create a line to that, or if they didn’t have the music I had to draw from things I had heard years ago, like the old standards. That’s where I learned most of those, just by playing with other groups over a period of time.
